name: Build a fully restricted pod + enforce PSA
objective: CKS › Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities. Drill EVERY pod-hardening corner harder than the exam: runAsNonRoot/runAsUser, drop-ALL capabilities, readOnlyRootFilesystem, seccomp RuntimeDefault, privilege-escalation lockdown, a fully restricted-compliant pod, Pod Security Admission (enforce + audit/warn, pinned), and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: A fully restricted-compliant pod
questions.teach:
The *restricted* Pod Security Standard wants **all** of: `runAsNonRoot: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `capabilities.drop: [ALL]`, and `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault`. Combine them so the pod would pass under `enforce=restricted`.

**Gotcha:** restricted requires `capabilities.drop` contain **ALL** (not just a few caps) and forbids adding anything except `NET_BIND_SERVICE`.
questions.prompt:
Create pod `restricted-app` in `cks-podsec` (image `busybox:1.36`, container `app`, `sleep 3600`) that satisfies the *restricted* standard:
- pod-level `runAsNonRoot: true`, `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault`
- container `runAsUser: 1000`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `capabilities.drop: [ALL]`

Target: every field above is set as specified.
questions.hint: Put `runAsNonRoot` + `seccompProfile` under `spec.securityContext`; put `runAsUser`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, and `capabilities.drop:[ALL]` under the container `securityContext`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: restricted-app, namespace: cks-podsec }
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      runAsUser: 1000
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
YAML
questions.eli5:
Think of airport security with escalating levels of screening. **Privileged** is the VIP lane — walk straight through, no checks. **Baseline** is normal screening — stops the obviously dangerous stuff. **Restricted** is the strictest line: full-body scan, everything by the book. The *restricted* Pod Security Standard is that strictest line for pods.

To get a pod through the restricted lane, it has to pass **a whole checklist at once** — not just one item:

- **Not a root traveler** — `runAsNonRoot: true` (pod level) and a real non-zero `runAsUser: 1000` (container level).
- **Can't upgrade your pass mid-flight** — `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`.
- **Surrendered the whole keyring** — `capabilities.drop: [ALL]`.
- **Using the house syscall filter** — `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault`.

This step is about assembling **all** of those into one pod so it would sail through `enforce=restricted`. Miss any single item and the whole pod gets turned away at the gate.

**Watch out:**

- **restricted needs `capabilities.drop` to contain `ALL`** — dropping just a few named caps isn't enough.
- The **only** capability you may `add` back is `NET_BIND_SERVICE`; adding anything else fails restricted.
- Fields live at **two levels**: `runAsNonRoot` + `seccompProfile` go under the **pod** `securityContext`; `runAsUser`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, and `capabilities.drop` go under the **container** `securityContext`. Container settings win if they clash.
- `runAsNonRoot: true` with no non-zero `runAsUser` still fails to start a root image like busybox — you need both.
- It's all-or-nothing: one missing field means the pod violates restricted.
questions.deepDive:
## A fully restricted-compliant pod — full rundown

### Mental model
The **restricted** Pod Security Standard is the strictest of the three built-in profiles (privileged → baseline → restricted). A pod is compliant only when it satisfies **every** control at once. This lesson builds that pod by hand so it would pass `enforce=restricted`.

### What restricted requires (the checklist)
| Control | Required value | Level |
|---|---|---|
| Run as non-root | `runAsNonRoot: true` | pod or container |
| Non-zero UID | `runAsUser: <non-zero>` (needed so a root image starts) | container |
| No privilege escalation | `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` | container |
| Drop capabilities | `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` | container |
| Allowed added cap | only `NET_BIND_SERVICE` (or none) | container |
| seccomp | `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` (or `Localhost`) | pod or container |
| Not privileged | `privileged: false` (not `true`) | container |
| Host namespaces | `hostNetwork`/`hostPID`/`hostIPC` must be false/unset | pod |
| volume types | restricted to a safe set (configMap, emptyDir, PVC, secret, projected, downwardAPI, ephemeral) | pod |

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: restricted-app, namespace: cks-podsec }
spec:
  securityContext:                     # POD level
    runAsNonRoot: true
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:                   # CONTAINER level
      runAsUser: 1000
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
```

### Pod vs container placement
- **Pod-level** (`spec.securityContext`): `runAsNonRoot`, `seccompProfile` — set once, inherited by all containers.
- **Container-level** (`spec.containers[].securityContext`): `runAsUser`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation`, `capabilities` — note `capabilities` has **no** pod-level form.
- On conflict, **container-level wins** for that container.

### Verify against the real policy
The surest check is to try it in a namespace that enforces restricted:
```bash
kubectl label ns test pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --overwrite
kubectl -n test apply -f restricted-app.yaml   # should be admitted, no warnings
```
Or inspect the stored fields:
```bash
kubectl -n cks-podsec get pod restricted-app -o jsonpath='{.spec.securityContext}'; echo
kubectl -n cks-podsec get pod restricted-app -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext}'; echo
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`drop` must contain `ALL`** — dropping a few named caps is not restricted-compliant.
- **Only `NET_BIND_SERVICE` may be added back**; any other `add` fails.
- **`runAsNonRoot: true` + no non-zero `runAsUser`** still won't start busybox (defaults to UID 0).
- **seccomp must not be `Unconfined`** anywhere — restricted needs `RuntimeDefault`/`Localhost` on pod or every container.
- **All-or-nothing:** a single missing field makes the pod violate the profile under `enforce`.
- `privileged: true`, any `hostNetwork/hostPID/hostIPC`, or an unsafe volume type each break restricted independently.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      runAsUser: 1000
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
```

questions.title: Pod Security Admission: enforce + audit, pinned
questions.teach:
**Pod Security Admission** applies a Pod Security Standard per namespace via labels. `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=<level>` rejects violating pods; `audit`/`warn` only log/warn. Pin each mode with its `*-version` label so policy won't drift on upgrade.

**Gotcha:** `enforce` only checks pods at create/update — it does **not** evict pods already running.
questions.prompt:
Label namespace `cks-locked` to **enforce** `restricted` pinned to `v1.30`, and additionally **audit** at `baseline` pinned to `v1.30`.

Target: labels `enforce=restricted`, `enforce-version=v1.30`, `audit=baseline`, `audit-version=v1.30`.
questions.eli5:
A **namespace** is like a room in a building, and **Pod Security Admission (PSA)** is a doorkeeper you can post at that room's door. You tell the doorkeeper the house rules just by **sticking labels on the door** — no config files, no extra software. The rules come from the three standard rulebooks: *privileged* (anything goes), *baseline* (basic sanity), *restricted* (strict).

The doorkeeper can act in three different moods, and you can set several at once:

- **enforce** — the strict bouncer: a pod that breaks the rules is **turned away** (rejected, never created).
- **audit** — the quiet clipboard: lets everyone in but **writes violations into the log** for later review.
- **warn** — the polite heads-up: lets the pod in but **prints a warning** back to whoever ran the command.

Here you post two moods on the `cks-locked` room: **enforce at restricted** (strictly block bad pods) and **audit at baseline** (quietly log anything that wouldn't even meet the looser baseline bar). And crucially, you **pin the rulebook edition** with a `*-version` label (`v1.30`) so a cluster upgrade can't silently change what the rules mean.

**Watch out:**

- **enforce only checks pods at create/update time — it does NOT evict pods already running.** Label a busy namespace and the existing bad pods keep running; only new/updated ones get blocked.
- Each mode is its **own label**, and each gets its own **`-version` label**. Pin all of them or policy drifts on upgrade.
- The label key is exactly `pod-security.kubernetes.io/<mode>` and `.../<mode>-version` — a typo means the label is silently ignored.
- Use `--overwrite` or the label command fails if the key already exists.
- You can mix levels across modes (enforce restricted + audit baseline) — they're independent.
questions.deepDive:
## Pod Security Admission: enforce + audit, pinned — full rundown

### Mental model
**Pod Security Admission (PSA)** is a built-in admission controller (GA since 1.25) that applies the **Pod Security Standards** to a namespace. It's configured entirely with **namespace labels** — no CRDs, no extra deployment. You pick a **mode** (what happens on violation) and a **level** (which standard), and optionally **pin a version**.

### The three modes
| Mode | On violation | Affects running pods? |
|---|---|---|
| `enforce` | Pod is **rejected** at admission | ❌ no — create/update only |
| `audit` | Pod is **allowed**, violation recorded in the **audit log** | ❌ |
| `warn` | Pod is **allowed**, a **warning** is returned to the user/client | ❌ |

All three are independent and can be set simultaneously, each at its own level.

### The three levels
| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `privileged` | Unrestricted — no checks |
| `baseline` | Blocks known privilege escalations (no hostNetwork, no privileged, etc.) |
| `restricted` | Heavily hardened — runAsNonRoot, drop ALL caps, seccomp RuntimeDefault, no privilege escalation |

### The label schema
```
pod-security.kubernetes.io/<mode>=<level>
pod-security.kubernetes.io/<mode>-version=<v1.NN | latest>
```
`<mode>` ∈ {enforce, audit, warn}; `<level>` ∈ {privileged, baseline, restricted}. The `-version` pins the *edition* of the standard so policy doesn't drift when the cluster upgrades.

### The command for this task
```bash
kubectl label ns cks-locked \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.30 \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-version=v1.30 \
  --overwrite
```

### Verify
```bash
kubectl get ns cks-locked --show-labels
# or precisely:
kubectl get ns cks-locked -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}' | tr ',' '\n' | grep pod-security
```
Expected: `enforce=restricted`, `enforce-version=v1.30`, `audit=baseline`, `audit-version=v1.30`.

### A common real-world rollout pattern
Dry-run before enforcing: set `warn`/`audit` to the target level first to find offenders, then switch `enforce` on.
```bash
kubectl label ns cks-locked \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted --overwrite
# review warnings, fix pods, then add enforce=restricted
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`enforce` is create/update only — it does NOT evict already-running pods.** Existing violators keep running; only new/modified pods are blocked. Use `warn`/`audit` to *discover* existing violators.
- **Each mode needs its own `-version` label** to be pinned; forgetting it leaves that mode on `latest` and subject to drift.
- **Exact label key** `pod-security.kubernetes.io/...` — a typo (e.g. missing `.io`) is silently accepted as an unrelated label and does nothing.
- **`--overwrite`** is required when the labels already exist, or the command errors.
- Modes are **independent** — you can enforce one level and audit/warn another (e.g. enforce restricted, audit baseline).
- PSA acts on **pods** — it doesn't directly reject Deployments, but the Deployment's pods fail to create, surfacing in the ReplicaSet/Deployment events.
- The `kube-system` namespace is typically exempt via PSA configuration.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl label ns cks-locked \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.30 \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-version=v1.30 --overwrite

kubectl get ns cks-locked --show-labels
```
